blocks.text: It is proved that תחמס thachmas is the male ostrich.

Just as among the Greeks ἅρπη [harpē], ἁρπετὸς [harpetos], ἁρπυία [harpyia] are names of birds of prey, so called from seizing [col. 232], so among the unclean birds forbidden in the Law, תחמס thachmas is believed to be one of the birds of prey, because חמס chamas, from which thachmas comes, means to seize and to do violence. This is roughly the view of the more recent Hebrews. Kimchi: נקרא כן שחומס שאר העופות וגוזל אותם, It is so called because it does violence to the other birds and seizes them. Aquinas: תחמס שם עוף דורס, Thachmas, the name of a bird of prey. Pomarius: עוף דורסים פלקוני בלעז או כדומה, A bird of the raptor kind, falcon in the vernacular, or another similar to it. Accordingly Arias renders it hawk. Among the ancients, Jonathan and the Jerusalem translator seemed to support this view; they have here חטפיתא chataphitha, or חטופיתא chatupphitha, which most lexicographers hold to be the name of a bird of prey, because חטף means to seize. So Kimchi confirms from the Jerusalem Paraphrase what he had said, that תחמס thachmas is a bird of prey. The Elders render it γλαῦκα [glauka], and Jerome little owl. Fuller strongly approves this version in Miscellanea book 6, chapter 9, and tries to confirm it from the etymology of the word, since it is characteristic of the little owl both to do violence and to suffer it, as the other birds vie in flying at it. Perhaps also in Onkelos ציצא tsitsa is the little owl, as in Greek τυτώ [tytō]. Hesychius: Τυτώ· ἡ γλαύξ [Tytō: hē glaux]. From ציצא tsitsa came τυτώ [tytō], as τύρος [tyros] from צור tsor, and τάνις [tanis] from צען tsoan. Or ציצא tsitsa and τυτὼ [tytō] are onomatopoeic words, ὀνοματοποιητικὰ [onomatopoiētika], which [II, 831] seem to imitate the hooting of the little owl. To this belongs the joke of Plautus in the Menaechmi, Act 4.
M. Who is this Menaechmus? P. YOU, I say. M. I? P. YOU, etc. M. Did I give it? P. YOU there, I say. Shall I have a little owl brought, to keep saying TUTU at you? For we are already done for.

Therefore I would also rather explain the Arabs' طوط [ṭwṭ] taut as little owl than, with Giggeius, as bat ^{(1)}. Here I deliberately pass over those who render תחמס as harpe, or harpy, or cymindis, or nycticorax: both because they are not of much weight, and because, as far as I know, they offer no reasons for their interpretation except this one alone, namely that the name of the bird תחמס thachmas is derived from robbery.

But this was the τὸ πρῶτον ψεῦδος [to prōton pseudos] that led most interpreters astray: they thought that חמס chamas and חטף chataph were wholly synonymous. I admit they are of neighbouring meaning, but I flatly deny that they mean the same. Properly חטף chataph is to seize; חמס chamas, to act unjustly. For you would not correctly render עד חמס ^{a)}, so frequent in the sacred text, as witness of robbery, but witness of iniquity, that is, unjust and false. Likewise חמסו תורה ^{b)} you should not render they have seized the Law, but they have acted unjustly against the Law. And elsewhere: Against the orphan and the widow אל תחמסו ^{c)}, do not act unjustly. Again: He who offends against wisdom חומס נפשו ^{d)} acts unjustly against himself. So in the Psalms חמס is everywhere joined as a synonym with עמל, עולה, תוך, רע and רשע. And the Septuagint never renders חמס as ἁρπαγὴν [harpagēn], but as ἀδίκημα [adikēma], ἀδικίαν [adikian], ἀθεσίαν [athesian], ἀνομίαν [anomian], ὄνειδος [oneidos], ὕβριν [hybrin]. And indeed, wherever חמס means to seize or to do violence, it is so taken only by consequence [col. 233], because extorting something by force against law and right is the conduct of unjust men. Therefore there is no need for תחמס to be a bird of prey, in Hebrew עוף דורס, since it has been proved that the word חמס properly signifies what is impious and unjust, even in one free of the crime of rapacity. So whatever bird is said to be תחמס thachmas will answer well enough to the name, if it is proved to be unjust and impious, [II, 832] even if it is not counted among the birds of prey. Moreover, no bird has so bad a name for impiety as the ostrich. The others take care to brood their eggs and rear their young; this one leaves her eggs on the ground, to be warmed in the dust, and does not consider that a foot may crush them and a beast of the field trample them. She is harsh toward her young, as if they were not hers; Iob. XXXIX, 17. 18. 19. Accordingly Jeremiah, Thren. IV, 3., takes an example of similar cruelty from the ostrich, as we have already touched on in passing and will explain more fully in expounding the words of Job.
